Tide (1950s print advert)

A bookmarkable reference page for media language and representation. Use it to learn the key ideas, then to plan close textual analysis answers.

BrandProcter & Gamble
ProductHeavy-duty machine washing powder
Launched1946 (advertised heavily through the 1950s)
AgencyD’Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles (DMB&B)
FormPrint advert, consumer product

How to use this page

  1. Learn: work through the six toolkit sections. Each has a definition and an “In Tide” example.
  2. Stretch: open “Going further” for the wider theory, links between theorists and evaluation points.
  3. Practise: in “See it in action”, notice the pattern sign → denotation → connotation → underlying idea. Use it in every exam paragraph.
  4. Check: use the theorist grid for quick revision of who argued what.

Core toolkit

Six key ideas for analysing Tide

1

Denotation, connotation and myth Barthes

Definition

Denotation is what we literally see or read. Connotation is the ideas, feelings and associations an audience attaches to it. For Barthes, myth is what happens when connotations become so familiar that an ideology (a set of beliefs about how the world is or should be) seems natural, like common sense.

In Tide
  • Denotation: a smiling woman with hair rolls and a headband hugs a box of Tide; pink hearts float above it.
  • Connotation: the hug and hearts connote love and devotion; bright primary red, yellow and blue connote positivity; red lipstick and full make-up connote idealised femininity.
  • Myth: the headline presents it as plain fact that women want a washing product. A woman’s happiness and fulfilment seem naturally tied to housework.
Exam moveAlways travel the same road: what I see → what it suggests → the wider idea it supports.
2

Anchorage and the narrative codes Barthes

Definition

Anchorage is when written text fixes the meaning of an image, narrowing the many possible meanings to one preferred meaning. Barthes’ five codes describe how texts create meaning and keep audiences interested:

  • Hermeneutic (enigma): a question or mystery that holds attention until it is answered.
  • Proairetic (action): signs that build tension and make us expect something to happen.
  • Semantic: connotations attached to particular signifiers.
  • Symbolic: larger themes, often built on contrasts such as good/bad.
  • Cultural: references to knowledge the audience is assumed to share.
CodeIn Tide
HermeneuticThe headline asks, in effect, “what do women want?” and the product is the answer.
ProaireticRepeated exclamation marks build tension and urgency; “Remember!” prompts an action (buying).
SemanticThe hearts and the woman’s hug connote love and relationship: she loves Tide as much as we are invited to.
SymbolicHyperbole and superlatives (“world’s cleanest wash!”) oppose Tide’s superior power to its rivals. Tide became brand leader by the mid-1950s.
Cultural“Washday” relies on shared knowledge of the weekly laundry routine; the Good Housekeeping seal and the Procter & Gamble name draw on trusted institutions.
In Tide: anchorage

On their own, the hearts and the hug could mean many things. The headline anchors them, so we read the embrace as proof that Tide is “what women want”.

3

Conventions of 1950s print adverts

Definition

Conventions are the familiar features audiences expect from a form or genre. Print adverts typically combine a headline, slogan, pack shot (image of the product), illustration, body copy and logo. In the 1950s, consumer culture was still developing and many brands were new, so adverts used more copy than modern ones to explain and persuade.

HyperboleExaggeration used to make a point, not to be taken literally.
SuperlativeLanguage suggesting the highest quality possible (cleanest, whitest).
TriplingGrouping three items or claims for rhythm and persuasion.
ImperativeA command (“Remember!”) that tells the audience what to do.
LexisChoice of words. Informal lexis is chatty (“sudsing whizz”); formal is serious.
TypographySans-serif connotes informality; serif connotes seriousness and fact.
In Tide
  • Hyperbole and superlatives: “World’s cleanest wash!”, “World’s whitest wash!” and “Washing miracle”.
  • Tripling: “No soap – no other ‘suds’ – no other washing product known”, plus the three-point “Only Tide does all three” list.
  • Typography: headline, subheadings and slogans are sans-serif (friendly, informal); the technical details are in serif (serious, factual).
  • Informal lexis: the comic-strip speech bubble “Tide’s a sudsing whizz” sounds like everyday talk.
  • Composition: a Z-line and rough rule of thirds guide the eye from the headline, across the pack, down to the slogan.
  • Colour: bright primary colours connote the positive associations the producers want us to link with the product.
4

Modes of address

Definition

Mode of address is the way a text speaks to its audience, through its tone, its language and where characters look.

  • Direct: speaks to “you”, using second-person pronouns, commands, questions or eye contact with the audience.
  • Indirect: lets the audience observe characters who are not addressing them, so we “overhear” or look on.
  • Tone can also be formal or informal.
Direct mode of addressIndirect mode of address
  • “No wonder you women buy more Tide…”
  • “Your wash”, “you can buy”
  • The imperative “Remember!” with a small figure pointing out at us
  • The woman at the washing machine (top right) in your class notes
  • The main woman hugging the box, absorbed in her feelings, not addressing us
  • The two women on the washing line talking to each other in the comic strip
In Tide: effects
  • Direct address creates engagement and a personal, authoritative tone: “Remember!” sounds like advice or an instruction from a trusted friend.
  • Indirect address presents the central woman as a role model. We watch her happiness with Tide and want it for ourselves. It also suggests her relationship with the product is what matters most.
  • Together they make the advert feel both intimate and persuasive.
Active learning taskExplain the effects of direct and indirect modes of address in the Tide advert. Aim for one quotation or visual detail for each, then explain the effect on the audience.
5

Representation Hall

Definition

For Stuart Hall, representation is the production of meaning through language, images and signs. Media do not simply reflect reality; they construct versions of it through selection and combination. Stereotypes reduce groups to a few simple characteristics. Meanings work because a culture shares a conceptual map of ideas.

In Tide: the housewife
  • Hair: waves, curls and rolls made fashionable by film stars such as Veronica Lake, Betty Grable and Rita Hayworth. Shorter hair also had a wartime, practical origin: long hair was hazardous around machinery in factories and farms.
  • Headband or scarf: links to practical wartime dress. Here the held-back hair connotes focus on her work, though this is arguably opposed by her full make-up.
  • Clothing and setting: polka-dot blouse, apron and full skirt; washing machine and washing line.
  • Who is missing: there are no men and no other kinds of women. Men appear only as clothes on the line, so family laundry is shown as a woman’s job.
  • Shared conceptual map: the domestic scenes are familiar to the audience as images of their own lives, so the stereotype feels normal.
Context

During WWII women filled jobs vacated by men (see the Rosie the Riveter and Women’s Land Army adverts in “Going further”). In the post-war consumer boom, advertising for home technology targeted women as housewives, while men were targeted for products such as cars. Tide chooses to reinforce the domestic stereotype rather than challenge it.

6

Binary oppositions Lévi-StraussA Level

Definition

Claude Lévi-Strauss argued that we make sense of texts through binary oppositions: pairs of opposites such as good/evil or clean/dirty. Each side is understood by contrast with the other, and audiences are guided to value one side over the other.

OppositionWhere it appears in Tide
Tide / rival products“Cleaner than any other washday product”; “There’s nothing like Procter & Gamble’s Tide”; “unlike soap”; whiter than “any soap or washing product known”.
Clean / dirty“As clean as Tide!” implies the unclean wash that other products leave behind.
New / old-fashioned“New washing miracle” against ordinary soap.
Work / femininityHair held back for work, but full make-up and a glamorous look (see Hall, Section 5).
Domestic woman / working womanIntertext: Tide’s housewife against the wartime “We Can Do It!” and Land Army women.
In Tide

The advert asks us to choose a side: Tide is clean, new and trusted; everything else is inferior. This links straight back to Barthes’ symbolic code (Section 2).

Going further

The wider theory behind the toolkit

Use this section to move into top-band answers: connect theorists to each other, and evaluate how useful each theory is for Tide.

Hall: encoding, decoding and reception

Audiences do not all read a text in the same way. Hall describes three positions:

ReadingMeaningApplied to Tide
Preferred (dominant)Accepts the intended meaningWomen are the main consumers of Tide; it is the best product and can be trusted. Words like “trust”, “truly safe”, “miracle” and “nothing like” reassure, and the Good Housekeeping seal confirms it.
NegotiatedAccepts part, adapts partTide may well clean well, but the claim that it is “what women want” goes too far.
OppositionalRejects the intended meaningThe advert reveals a patriarchal agenda that confines women to housework, especially to women who had worked outside the home during the war.

Links: Gauntlett (do audiences accept the identity on offer?) · Barthes (the encoded sign) · Gerbner (does repetition make the preferred reading seem natural?)

Gauntlett: identity and “pick and mix”

David Gauntlett argues that people use media as a resource to construct their identities, “picking and mixing” from the range of representations on offer. He contrasts today’s wider choice of role models with older media that gave narrow, prescriptive messages about how men and women should be.

In Tide

The women in the advert are role models of domestic perfection: happy, glamorous and in control of the laundry. They offer one identity to buy into. But women who had worked during the war might refuse this and turn to products and role models that reflected a more challenging life.

Links: Hall (shared conceptual map versus individual identity) · van Zoonen (gender constructed) · hooks (whose identities are missing)

van Zoonen: feminist theory and gender

Liesbet van Zoonen argues that gender is constructed through media representations rather than being natural, and that the media can contribute to social change by representing women in non-traditional roles and avoiding sexist language.

In Tide

Social roles for women had shifted during the war, but the advert does the opposite of what van Zoonen says the media can do. It frames laundry as women’s work, speaks for “women” as one group and glamorises the housewife.

Links: Hall (stereotyping) · Gauntlett (role models) · compare Kiss of the Vampire (Section A), where van Zoonen’s “spectacle” and challenges to stereotype are both in play.

bell hooks and Gilroy: intersectionality and otherness

bell hooks argues that gender cannot be separated from race and class (intersectionality) and examines how patriarchal oppression works alongside other forms of power. She notes that western ideals of beauty favour lighter-skinned women. Paul Gilroy’s postcolonial approach asks how media texts position some groups as the norm and others as “other”, and how they can reinforce colonial-era power.

In Tide
  • Every woman shown is white, “modern”, apparently middle-class and part of a heterosexual household. This is presented as the default woman.
  • Women of colour, and women whose lives did not fit the housewife ideal, are absent. Their exclusion makes the “normal” woman seem universal.
  • Context: WWII had challenged traditional power structures, so the advert’s picture of a settled “modern” white woman can be read as reasserting an older order.

Links: van Zoonen (whose representations are missing?) · Hall (stereotyping and “shared” maps that exclude) · Barthes (myth of the universal woman)

Bandura and Gerbner: media effects

Albert Bandura’s social learning theory suggests that people learn by observing and imitating models, especially models who are rewarded. George Gerbner’s cultivation theory argues that long-term, repeated exposure to consistent media messages gradually shapes how people see the world.

In Tide
  • Bandura: the central woman is rewarded with love, pleasure and glamour for her devotion to Tide, which models the behaviour for female viewers.
  • Gerbner: DMB&B ran print and radio campaigns for Tide at the same time, repeating the same housewife character and the idea that customers “loved” Tide. Repeated across many 1950s adverts, this could make the brand-leader message and the housewife role seem normal.

Same-era adverts: the same representation repeated

Links: Hall (shared conceptual maps built through repetition) · Gauntlett (is the audience passive?) · see evaluation below

Contrasting representations: the wartime intertexts

Intertextual comparison shows that representation is a choice. Wartime campaigns showed women in roles outside the home because society needed them there; Tide reinforces the domestic role afterwards.

Links: Hall (selection and combination) · van Zoonen (media and social change) · Lévi-Strauss (working woman / domestic woman)

Evaluation points for exam answers

  • Barthes versus Hall: semiotics is powerful for close reading but can treat meaning as fixed in the text. Hall adds that audiences decode in different ways.
  • Judge by the period: from today’s view the advert looks sexist, but in the 1950s this was the accepted “norm”. Remember that oppositional readings still existed, especially among women who had worked in the war.
  • Gauntlett’s challenge: if audiences pick and mix identities, representations may have less power than Bandura and Gerbner suggest.
  • Effects theories: Tide’s sales success does not prove it changed anyone’s beliefs. Women may also have chosen it for practical reasons.
  • Reflect or construct? Does the advert mirror 1950s society, or help create the idea that housework is women’s work? A strong answer argues for both and uses evidence.

Applying the ideas

Tide: sign → denotation → connotation → underlying idea

SignDenotationConnotationUnderlying idea
Hearts above the boxPink outlined heartsLove, affection, devotionWomen are “naturally” devoted to domestic products (myth). Barthes’ semantic code.
Woman hugging the Tide boxSmiling housewife embracing the pack, not looking at usPassion for the product; the product as something preciousFulfilment through housework; indirect address makes her a role model (Gauntlett).

Extra example 1: Kiss of the Vampire poster (1963) Section A

A monster-movie poster from the decade of women’s liberation, mixing old and new representations of women.

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
Woman on the left: on her knees, throat bare, head backHeld by the male vampire; connotes submission and lack of powerReinforces the stereotype of woman as victim (Hall).
Woman on the right: aggressive expression, holding a kneeling manConnotes power and dominance; the man is the victimChallenges stereotype, reflecting 1960s women challenging male dominance (Gauntlett, van Zoonen).
Long, silky, light dressesEmphasise curves; connote femininity and delicacyWomen as spectacle for a male audience (van Zoonen).
Dark palette with red for bats and bloodGloom, danger, and romance (“Kiss”)Genre conventions; enigma around the vampires’ relationship (hermeneutic code).
Compare with Tide: both posters and adverts construct femininity. Tide reinforces one stereotype and is aimed at women as consumers; Kiss of the Vampire mixes reinforced and challenged stereotypes for a mainly male assumed audience.

Extra example 2: Super. Human. (Channel 4, Tokyo 2020) Section A

An audio-visual advert for the Paralympic Games that challenges stereotypes of disabled people.

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
Time-lapse bruise and close-up shotsUncomfortable, realistic detail; the physical cost of trainingAthletes as ordinary “human” people, not just “super”; neither victims nor heroes.
No voice-over or moralising graphicsThe stories are shown, not explainedAuthenticity; audiences make their own meaning.
“So You Want To Be a Boxer” (Bugsy Malone)Upbeat, familiar song; connotes struggle and hard work paying offIntertextual, humorous tone that invites audiences in.
“To be a Paralympian there’s got to be something wrong with you”Provocative closing statementChallenges audiences to examine their misconceptions about disability.
Compare with Tide: Tide tells women what they want with an anchoring headline and direct commands; Super. Human. shows and leaves audiences to draw conclusions. Who gets to define identity in each text (Gauntlett)? Which challenges the shared conceptual map and which reinforces it (Hall)?
Quick revision

Theorist grid

Roland Barthes

Media language

Semiotics. Denotation and connotation, myth (naturalised ideology), anchorage and the five narrative codes.

Tide: hearts connote love; headline anchors the image; “what women want” as myth.

Claude Lévi-Strauss

Media language

Structuralism. Meaning is made through binary oppositions that audiences understand by contrast.

Tide: Tide versus rival products; clean versus dirty; new versus old.

Stuart Hall

Representation · Audiences

Representation constructs meaning and can stereotype; shared conceptual maps. Reception theory: preferred, negotiated and oppositional readings.

Tide: the housewife stereotype; preferred reading is trust in Tide.

David Gauntlett

Representation

Identity is built by “picking and mixing” from media resources. Older media offered narrower role models.

Tide: role model of domestic perfection that audiences may accept or reject.

Liesbet van Zoonen

Representation

Feminist theory. Gender is constructed in media, which can contribute to social change through non-traditional representations.

Tide: reinforces rather than challenges women’s domestic role.

bell hooks

Representation

Intersectionality (gender, race and class together) and patriarchal oppression. Western beauty ideals favour lighter-skinned women.

Tide: only white, “modern” women represented as the norm.

Paul Gilroy

Representation

Postcolonial theory. Ethnicity and “otherness”: how media position some groups as the default and others as outsiders.

Tide: whiteness unmarked as the default; other groups absent.

Albert Bandura

Audiences

Media effects. People learn by observing and imitating media models, especially rewarded behaviour.

Tide: the happy housewife models behaviour for female viewers.

George Gerbner

Audiences

Cultivation theory. Long-term, repeated exposure shapes people’s view of reality.

Tide: repeated housewife and brand-leader messages across print and radio.

Curran & Seaton

Industries

Media ownership and power. Ownership concentrated in few hands affects content; commercial pressures such as advertising shape media.

Link: advertising funds commercial media, including newspapers.

Livingstone & Lunt

Industries

Regulation, and audiences positioned as citizens or as consumers.

Link: Tide addresses women purely as consumers.

David Hesmondhalgh

Industries

Cultural industries. Companies reduce risk by relying on proven formulas, stars, brands and sequels.

Link: a repeated formula of housewife, hyperbole and endorsement.

Henry Jenkins

Audiences

Fandom and participatory culture; audiences take and reshape texts (“textual poaching”).

Link: today’s audiences can respond to and remix adverts online.

Clay Shirky

Audiences

“The end of the audience”: digital tools make audiences into prosumers who create and share media.

Link: 1950s print audiences were one-way receivers; now they talk back.

Connections

Section A ↔ Section B

Close analysis of Tide (Section A) gives you language and examples for the industries and audiences questions in Section B.

  • Industries: DMB&B used the Procter & Gamble name in Tide campaigns because research showed consumers trusted the company, and ran print and radio campaigns together to build familiarity quickly. How does a company’s reputation work as a marketing tool?
  • Hesmondhalgh (risk minimisation): repeating a proven formula, such as the housewife character and hyperbolic claims, lowers commercial risk. Compare franchises and sequels (Assassin’s Creed, Black Panther) as the same strategy.
  • Curran & Seaton: advertising helps fund commercial media. Compare how newspapers such as the Daily Mirror and The Times depend on advertising and on attracting particular audiences.
  • Livingstone & Lunt: Tide positions women only as consumers, not citizens. Would a claim like “world’s cleanest wash” need evidence in today’s UK advertising regulation?
  • Audiences: Hall’s reception theory, Bandura and Gerbner (Section 5 of “Going further”) apply to newspapers too. Compare the Daily Mirror and The Times front pages (1 Feb 2022) using the same questions: how do they address their audience, and which reading is preferred?
  • Then versus now: 1950s print audiences could not reply. Shirky’s prosumers and Jenkins’ participatory culture explain how modern audiences can respond to, parody and share adverts.
